## Solution

We evaluate the infinite series

$$S = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\ln\left(1+x^{2^{n}}\right), \qquad |x|<1.$$

**Key identity.** For any $a$, the difference of squares gives

$$(1-a)(1+a)=1-a^{2}.$$

Setting $a = x^{2^{n}}$ and using $a^{2}=x^{2^{n}\cdot 2}=x^{2^{n+1}}$,

$$(1-x^{2^{n}})(1+x^{2^{n}})=1-x^{2^{n+1}},$$

so that, whenever the logarithms are defined,

$$\ln\!\left(1+x^{2^{n}}\right)=\ln\!\left(1-x^{2^{n+1}}\right)-\ln\!\left(1-x^{2^{n}}\right). \tag{1}$$

**Telescoping.** Summing (1) from $n=1$ to $N$,

$$\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ln\!\left(1+x^{2^{n}}\right)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\Big[\ln\!\left(1-x^{2^{n+1}}\right)-\ln\!\left(1-x^{2^{n}}\right)\Big].$$

The right-hand side is a telescoping sum. Writing out terms:

$$\bigl[\ln(1-x^{2^{2}})-\ln(1-x^{2^{1}})\bigr]+\bigl[\ln(1-x^{2^{3}})-\ln(1-x^{2^{2}})\bigr]+\cdots+\bigl[\ln(1-x^{2^{N+1}})-\ln(1-x^{2^{N}})\bigr],$$

all intermediate terms cancel, leaving

$$\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ln\!\left(1+x^{2^{n}}\right)=\ln\!\left(1-x^{2^{N+1}}\right)-\ln\!\left(1-x^{2}\right). \tag{2}$$

**Taking $N\to\infty$.** For $|x|<1$ we have $|x|^{2^{N+1}}\to 0$ (in fact super-exponentially fast), hence $x^{2^{N+1}}\to 0$ and

$$\ln\!\left(1-x^{2^{N+1}}\right)\longrightarrow \ln(1)=0.$$

Passing to the limit in (2),

$$S = \lim_{N\to\infty}\left[\ln\!\left(1-x^{2^{N+1}}\right)-\ln\!\left(1-x^{2}\right)\right]=0-\ln(1-x^{2}).$$

**Convergence domain.** The identity (1) requires $1-x^{2^{n}}>0$ for all $n\ge 1$. Since $|x|<1$ implies $0<x^{2^{n}}<1$ for every $n\ge 1$ (when $x\neq 0$; the case $x=0$ gives $S=\sum\ln 1=0$, consistent with the formula), the condition $|x|<1$ suffices. For $|x|\ge 1$ the general term $\ln(1+x^{2^{n}})$ does not tend to $0$, so the series diverges.

**Result.**

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\ln\left(1+x^{2^{n}}\right)=-\ln\!\left(1-x^{2}\right)=\ln\frac{1}{1-x^{2}},\qquad |x|<1.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
